posts.title: 71% save time but 38% trust it
posts.hook:
71% of developers say AI coding tools save them time.

Only 38% say the code quality improved.
posts.body:
71% of developers say AI coding tools save them time.

Only 38% say the code quality improved.

That gap is the entire story of AI tooling right now.

I see it in my own workflow. Claude Code generates a working enrichment script in 90 seconds that would've taken me 45 minutes. But if I don't review the output, it'll silently swallow errors, skip edge cases, or build something structurally wrong that passes every test I didn't write.

Speed without verification is just faster technical debt.

The developers getting real value aren't the ones who tab-complete the fastest. They're the ones who treat AI output like a junior engineer's first PR. Read every line. Question the architecture. Push back on the easy solution.

I run a simple gate now: after any AI-generated code block, I ask myself "would I mass-approve this if a contractor submitted it?" If the answer is no, I rewrite. Not patch. Rewrite.

The 33% gap between "faster" and "better" is a skill gap. Not in the AI. In the person reviewing.

remixes.label: speed-trap
remixes.hook:
AI coding tools have a speed problem.

Not that they're too slow. That they're too fast.
remixes.body:
AI coding tools have a speed problem.

Not that they're too slow. That they're too fast.

When something generates a working script in 90 seconds, your brain skips the part where it would normally catch structural issues. You see "it runs" and move on. That's the trap.

I timed myself last week. Claude Code produced an enrichment pipeline in under two minutes. Reviewing that pipeline properly took me 25 minutes. Reading every function. Checking error handling. Tracing the data flow. Testing edge cases the model never considered.

The review took longer than writing it from scratch would have.

But here's the thing. The review surfaced three silent failures that would have corrupted data in production. A swallowed API timeout. A missing null check on a field that's empty 8% of the time. A retry loop with no backoff that would have hammered a rate-limited endpoint.

The 90-second generation is real. The time savings are real. But only if you budget the review time that speed makes you want to skip.

The developers getting the most from AI coding tools aren't the ones generating the fastest. They're the ones who treat every output like a pull request from a junior developer who's confident but sometimes wrong.
remixes.cta: How much of your AI-assisted coding time is generation vs. review? What ratio works for you?

remixes.label: trust-calibration
remixes.hook:
The most important skill in AI-assisted development isn't prompting.

It's knowing when NOT to trust the output.
remixes.body:
The most important skill in AI-assisted development isn't prompting.

It's knowing when NOT to trust the output.

Stack Overflow's 2024 survey showed a 33-point gap between developers who say AI saves time and those who say it improves quality. That gap isn't a bug in the tools. It's a calibration problem in the humans using them.

I've developed a mental checklist after shipping AI-generated code for over a year. Three questions before anything goes to production:

1. Did I specify the failure modes, or just the happy path? If I only described what should happen, the model only built for what should happen.

2. Can I explain every line? If I can't trace the logic, I don't ship it. Period. Velocity means nothing if you're building on code you don't understand.

3. What did it assume? Every AI-generated function carries implicit assumptions about input shape, error behavior, and state. Those assumptions are rarely documented. Finding them is the job.

The teams I see struggling with AI code quality aren't bad at prompting. They're bad at reviewing. They treat the output like a finished product instead of a first draft that needs editing.

Time saved on generation, reinvested in review. That's the actual workflow.

posts.title: 50k emails 12 meetings replacement
posts.hook:
50,000 emails. 12 meetings.

That's not an outbound problem. That's an architecture problem.
posts.body:
50,000 emails. 12 meetings.

That's not an outbound problem. That's an architecture problem.

I've seen this exact scenario play out three times this year with companies I've worked with. The playbook is always the same: buy a list, load it into Smartlead, blast a sequence, wonder why reply rates are under 0.5%.

The 3-person GTM engineering team that replaces that motion looks like this:

🔧 One person owns signal collection. Job postings, funding rounds, tech stack changes, hiring patterns. Not a bought list. Live intent.

🔧 One person owns enrichment and scoring. Every account gets a relevance score before a single email sends. If the score is below threshold, it doesn't send. Period.

🔧 One person owns copy and infrastructure. Domain warming, mailbox rotation, deliverability monitoring. The plumbing nobody wants to maintain.

The difference isn't headcount. It's that every email has a reason to exist before it sends. You're not hoping 50,000 shots hit something. You're sending 2,000 emails to accounts where the timing actually makes sense.

Volume is the laziest growth lever. Precision is harder to build but it compounds.
posts.cta: If you stripped your outbound down to only signal-qualified sends, how many emails would actually go out?

The math on spray-and-pray outbound is finally broken enough that leadership is listening.

remixes.hook:

remixes.body:
Your outbound team sent 50,000 emails last quarter.

How many of those companies were actually hiring for the problem you solve?

When I ask this question, most founders go quiet. They don't know. Their list came from a data provider filtered by industry and headcount. Maybe company size. Maybe tech stack. But almost never filtered by "is this company experiencing the problem we solve right now."

That's the architecture problem with modern outbound. The infrastructure is sophisticated. Warmup domains, rotation schedules, deliverability monitoring, AI personalization. But the targeting is still spray-and-pray with better formatting.

The teams I've seen fix this start by defining 3 to 5 observable signals that correlate with their best customers. Job postings with specific keywords. Tech stack changes visible in BuiltWith. Funding rounds at a specific stage. Leadership changes in the buying department.

Then they build a pipeline that monitors those signals daily and only triggers outreach when a threshold is met. The volume drops by 90%. The reply rate goes up 8 to 12x. The meeting rate per email sent looks completely different.

50,000 emails to 12 meetings is a 0.024% conversion rate. 500 signal-qualified emails to 12 meetings is 2.4%. Same meetings. 100x better economics. Completely different infrastructure.
remixes.cta: What signals would tell you a company is experiencing your problem right now, not just fitting your ICP on paper?

Here's exactly what those three people do.

Person one builds the signal layer. They write scripts that monitor job boards, press releases, funding databases, and tech stack changes. When a target account shows buying behavior, it gets flagged. Not scored by a vendor's black box. Flagged by observable, explainable criteria your team defined.

Person two builds the enrichment and personalization layer. When a signal fires, they pull context. Who's the right contact. What's their LinkedIn activity saying. What did the company just announce. This becomes the raw material for outreach that references real events, not "I noticed your company is growing."

Person three builds the delivery infrastructure. Domain warming, rotation schedules, inbox placement monitoring, reply handling. They treat email delivery like a production system, not a SaaS dashboard.

The old model: 10 SDRs sending 200 emails each per day from templates. 2,000 daily emails. Maybe 5 replies. The new model: 500 signal-triggered, deeply personalized emails per day. 25 to 40 replies.

The math isn't close. And the 3-person team costs less than the 15-person team's base salaries alone, before you count the tool stack.

posts.title: Clay workflow vs owning the pipeline
posts.hook:
Everyone's sharing their Clay workflows.

Almost nobody owns the data those workflows produce.
posts.body:
Everyone's sharing their Clay workflows.

Almost nobody owns the data those workflows produce.

I built a hiring-intent enrichment pipeline last month. Job postings → role parsing → tech stack extraction → ICP scoring → CRM sync. Took about 6 hours to wire up with Claude Code, the Cluely API, and SQLite.

Could I have built it in Clay in 2 hours? Probably. But here's what I'd be renting:

→ The enrichment credits (per-row pricing adds up fast at scale)
→ The transformation logic (locked inside their UI)
→ The historical data (gone if I cancel)
→ The ability to run it on a cron at 2am without thinking about it

My version costs me API calls. Maybe $12/month for the volume I run. It sits in a SQLite database I can query however I want. I can plug in a new data source in 20 minutes because the schema is mine.

Clay is genuinely good for prototyping a workflow. But prototyping and production are different things. The moment a workflow drives real pipeline, I want to own every piece of it.

The build-vs-rent math has changed. A coding agent plus APIs plus SQLite replaces most of what the point-tool industry charges five figures for.

remixes.hook:

remixes.body:
You built a 47-step Clay workflow.

This isn't a Clay hit piece. It's a structural observation about where GTM teams are putting their operational knowledge.

Every time you build a workflow in a SaaS tool, you're encoding business logic into someone else's platform. The enrichment rules, the scoring criteria, the data transformations that make your pipeline work. All of it lives on their servers, governed by their API limits, their pricing tiers, their product decisions.

I built a hiring-intent enrichment pipeline last month. Job postings to role parsing to tech stack extraction to ICP scoring to CRM sync. Took about 6 hours with Claude Code and SQLite.

Could I have built it in Clay in 2 hours? Probably. But here's what I'd be renting: the enrichment logic runs on their compute, the data sits in their tables, the workflow breaks if they change their API or their pricing. And if I want to run it against 50,000 records instead of 5,000, I'm negotiating a contract upgrade.

With the local version, I own the logic, the data, and the execution. I can run it at 3am against any volume. I can modify it without checking a changelog. I can hand it to a client without a seat license.

The 4 extra hours bought me permanent infrastructure instead of a rental agreement.
remixes.cta: What's the most valuable workflow you've built inside a platform you don't control?

The GTM engineers I respect most run their pipelines from a SQLite database on their laptop.

Not because it's cool. Because it's theirs.

The shift from SaaS workflows to local-first GTM infrastructure is happening quietly. Nobody's announcing it on LinkedIn because there's no vendor to tag and no affiliate link to share. But the practitioners doing the best work have been migrating their critical logic out of platform tools for the past year.

Here's what local-first GTM actually looks like in practice:

Enrichment runs as a Python script, not a Clay column. You control the provider, the fallback logic, the retry behavior, and the cost per record. When an API changes, you update one function instead of rebuilding a 30-step workflow.

Scoring lives in a SQLite table with explicit weights you can version control. Not a black box inside a vendor's platform that you can't export or audit.

CRM sync is a script that runs on a schedule, with full logging and error handling you wrote yourself. Not a webhook chain that fails silently.

The tradeoff is real. This takes longer to build initially. You need to be comfortable with code or have someone on the team who is. But once it's built, you own it completely. No per-seat costs. No API rate limits you didn't choose. No vendor deciding to sunset the feature your pipeline depends on.

posts.title: One workflow 10x better
posts.hook:
The companies winning with AI agents picked one workflow and made it 10x better.

The companies losing picked twelve workflows and made them all 1.2x better.
posts.body:
The companies winning with AI agents picked one workflow and made it 10x better.

The companies losing picked twelve workflows and made them all 1.2x better.

I watched this pattern play out in my own work. Early on I tried to automate everything at once. Content generation, lead scoring, email personalization, CRM updates, analytics dashboards. All with agents. All at the same time.

Nothing shipped. Everything was 60% done.

Then I picked one thing: enrichment. Took a messy CSV of company domains and built a pipeline that pulls firmographics, tech stack, hiring signals, and news mentions... scores them against an ICP... and writes the qualified ones directly into Attio. One workflow. End to end.

That pipeline now runs every night. It's replaced a manual process that used to take 4 hours a week. The data quality is better because the enrichment sources are layered, not single-vendor.

Once that was solid, I moved to the next one. Then the next.

Sequential depth beats parallel breadth every time with agents. Each workflow you nail teaches you patterns that make the next one faster. But you have to actually nail it first.

remixes.body:
I automated 12 workflows with AI agents last year.

The only one that mattered was the one I almost didn't build.

It was a lead enrichment pipeline. Boring. Not flashy. No fancy multi-agent orchestration. Just: signal fires, pull context, score it, push to CRM. One workflow. One job.

I almost skipped it because I was busy building the other eleven. Content generation agents. Analytics dashboard automations. Email personalization engines. CRM update bots. Each one took a week to build and produced incremental improvements. Maybe 20% faster here, 15% less manual work there.

The enrichment pipeline took three weeks because I refused to move on until it was bulletproof. Every edge case handled. Every failure mode logged. Every output verified. Three weeks of focus on one thing.

That single pipeline now sources 60% of our qualified meetings. The other eleven automations combined account for maybe a 10% efficiency gain across the team.

The lesson cost me months: breadth of automation is seductive because it feels productive. You're always building, always shipping, always showing progress. But compounding value comes from depth. One workflow that's 10x better changes your business. Twelve workflows that are each 1.2x better change your dashboard.

The companies I see winning with AI agents figured this out faster than I did. They picked one workflow, made it exceptional, proved the ROI, and then expanded.
remixes.cta: What's the one workflow you keep half-building because you get distracted by the next automation idea?

remixes.label: 1.2x-trap

The 1.2x trap is killing AI agent adoption.

Here's how it works.
remixes.body:
The 1.2x trap is killing AI agent adoption.

Here's how it works.

You identify 10 workflows that could benefit from AI automation. Each one could save 20 minutes a day, reduce errors by 15%, or speed up a process by 30%. Individually, they're all reasonable projects.

So you build all of them. Simultaneously. With the same small team.

Six months later, you have 10 half-finished automations. Each one works "mostly." Each one needs babysitting. Each one saved some time but created new failure modes that need monitoring. The net result: you're busier than before, with more systems to maintain and no single transformation to point to.

This is the 1.2x trap. Small improvements spread across many workflows feel like progress but never compound into transformation.

Contrast this with the team that picked their highest-volume, most painful workflow and spent three months making it genuinely excellent. They didn't just automate it. They rethought it. They handled every edge case. They built monitoring. They measured obsessively.

That one workflow now runs at a level that wasn't possible before. It didn't just save 20 minutes. It changed what the team can do.

The difference isn't resources or talent. It's focus. One 10x workflow beats ten 1.2x workflows every time, because 10x changes behavior and 1.2x just changes the dashboard.

posts.title: RevOps is engineering now
posts.hook:
RevOps used to mean running reports in Salesforce.

Now it means writing Python scripts that move pipeline.
posts.body:
RevOps used to mean running reports in Salesforce.

Now it means writing Python scripts that move pipeline.

The shift happened quietly. First it was Clay tables replacing manual enrichment. Then n8n workflows replacing Zapier chains. Then coding agents replacing the Clay tables themselves.

I talk to RevOps people every week who are building their own enrichment pipelines, their own lead scoring models, their own attribution systems. Not because they want to be engineers. Because the tools they were paying for couldn't do what they needed.

The skill stack that matters now:

✅ Enough SQL to query your own warehouse
✅ Enough Python to glue APIs together
✅ Enough prompt engineering to make an agent do the tedious parts
✅ Enough infrastructure sense to keep it running at 2am without babysitting

You don't need a CS degree. You need a coding agent and a weekend. I've watched operators go from zero code to running their own prospecting pipeline in under a month.

The title is still RevOps. The job is GTM engineering. The people who figure that out first are going to be impossible to hire away from their current companies.
posts.cta: Are you seeing this shift on your team? RevOps people picking up code, or engineers moving into ops?

remixes.hook:

"Am I still in RevOps if I spend half my day writing Python?"
remixes.body:
A RevOps manager messaged me last week.

"Am I still in RevOps if I spend half my day writing Python?"

Yes. You're just in the version of RevOps that exists now, not the one you were hired for.

Two years ago, this person's job was Salesforce reports, dashboard maintenance, and data hygiene tickets. Standard ops work. Then they started building Clay tables to replace manual enrichment. Then they realized Clay was a bottleneck and started writing Python scripts to pull from APIs directly. Then they built a lead scoring model in SQLite because the CRM's native scoring was too rigid.

Now they spend 50% of their week writing code. Their title still says RevOps. Their work looks like engineering.

This is happening everywhere and it's creating a real career question. The RevOps people who learn to code are becoming dramatically more valuable. They understand the business context that pure engineers lack, and they can build the technical systems that pure ops people can't.

But most companies haven't updated their job descriptions, comp bands, or career ladders to reflect this. So you have RevOps people doing engineering work at ops salaries, or leaving for GTM engineer roles at companies that recognize the skillset.

The shift is structural, not a trend. As AI coding tools lower the barrier to building, more ops people will cross into engineering territory. The question isn't whether this happens. It's whether your org recognizes it.
remixes.cta: If you're in RevOps and writing code now, how did that transition start for you?

remixes.label: three-waves
remixes.hook:
RevOps has gone through three waves in two years.

Most teams are stuck in wave two.
remixes.body:
RevOps has gone through three waves in two years.

Most teams are stuck in wave two.

Wave one was the Salesforce era. RevOps meant report building, dashboard maintenance, and making sure the CRM data was clean. The tools were enterprise platforms. The skill was knowing where to click.

Wave two was the no-code era. Clay tables replaced manual enrichment. Zapier chains replaced hand-built integrations. n8n workflows replaced Zapier when it got expensive. The tools got faster, but the model was the same: configure a platform to do what you need.

Wave three is happening now, and it's different. Coding agents are replacing the platforms themselves. A RevOps person with Claude Code or Cursor can build a custom enrichment pipeline in an afternoon. Not configure someone else's tool. Build their own.

The gap between wave two and wave three is significant. Wave two RevOps rents capability from platforms. Wave three RevOps owns it. Wave two is constrained by what the tool supports. Wave three is constrained only by what you can think of and describe.

But here's why most teams are stuck: wave three requires writing code or at least being code-comfortable. And most RevOps people were hired for platform knowledge, not engineering skills. The ones making the jump are using AI coding tools as their bridge, going from "I know what to build" to "I can build it" in months instead of years.

posts.title: Content strategy vs content pipeline
posts.hook:
Most B2B content strategies produce content.

Very few produce pipeline.
posts.body:
Most B2B content strategies produce content.

Very few produce pipeline.

The difference isn't quality. It's distribution architecture.

I ran an experiment over 90 days. Same content. Two distribution paths.

Path A: publish blog post, share on LinkedIn, boost with ads. Standard playbook.

Path B: publish blog post, pull key insights into Reddit comments where people are actively asking about the topic, repurpose into a Substack newsletter with email capture, syndicate the tactical pieces to niche communities.

Path A generated 3x more impressions. Path B generated 7x more inbound conversations.

The difference is intent density. LinkedIn impressions are people scrolling. Reddit threads are people searching for solutions to problems they have right now. Newsletter subscribers opted in because the last piece solved something.

I stopped measuring content by reach. I measure it by conversations started. A post that gets 200 views but lands in front of 5 people actively evaluating solutions is worth more than 20,000 impressions from people who double-tap and scroll.

Owned audience on a platform where people are solving problems beats rented reach on a platform where people are performing.
posts.cta: Where does your best pipeline actually come from? Not your most visible content. Your most converting.

inspired_by.author: Anthony Kennada
inspired_by.summary: Most B2B content strategies are SEO plays dressed up as thought leadership. The brands actually winning pipeline from content in 2025 are doing something different: they're building owned audiences that their competitors' ads can't reach. Newsletter → community → product-led sales is the motion. Not blog → rank → convert.

remixes.hook:
I tracked where 47 closed-won deals actually came from last quarter.

Only 3 started with a blog post someone read on our site.
remixes.body:
I tracked where 47 closed-won deals actually came from last quarter.

Only 3 started with a blog post someone read on our site.

The rest? Reddit threads where I dropped a real answer to a real question. Slack communities where I shared a framework without a pitch. LinkedIn comments where I added something the original poster missed.

None of that shows up in your content calendar. None of it gets a Canva graphic. Your content team would never put it in a monthly report because it looks like "just commenting."

But it converts at 8x the rate of a promoted blog post. Because the context is different. Someone asking "how do I solve X" on Reddit is further down the buying journey than someone scrolling past your thought leadership.

The insight that changed my approach: content isn't a funnel stage. It's a vehicle. And the vehicle matters less than where you park it.

I stopped measuring content by impressions and started measuring by conversations started. Pipeline followed.
remixes.cta: Pull up your last 10 closed-won deals. How many actually started from your "content strategy"?

remixes.label: reverse-engineering-pipeline
remixes.hook:
Your content calendar is full.

Your pipeline is empty.

These two facts are connected.
remixes.body:
Your content calendar is full.

Your pipeline is empty.

These two facts are connected.

Content calendars optimize for consistency. Pipeline optimizes for placement. These are different problems with different solutions.

Consistency means: publish Tuesday and Thursday, alternate formats, hit your keyword targets. It's a production schedule.

Placement means: find the 12 places where your buyers are already asking questions this week and show up with something useful. It's a distribution habit.

I worked with a B2B team that published 4 posts a week for 6 months. Solid writing. Good topics. Zero attributable pipeline. We killed the calendar and replaced it with a "signal scanner." Every morning, one person spent 30 minutes finding live conversations in Reddit, Slack, and LinkedIn comments where their ICP was asking for help.

They'd pull from existing content, reframe the insight for the conversation, and drop it in. No link. No pitch. Just the answer.

Pipeline tripled in 60 days. Content output dropped by 70%.

The bottleneck was never creation. It was placement.
remixes.cta: What percentage of your content team's time goes to creation vs. distribution? Be honest.

posts.title: Solo builder MRR reality check
posts.hook:
$5k MRR as a solo builder sounds like freedom.

It's actually the hardest revenue to maintain.
posts.body:
$5k MRR as a solo builder sounds like freedom.

It's actually the hardest revenue to maintain.

I've been there. You hit a number that covers rent and you think you've won. Then two customers churn in the same week and you realize there's no team absorbing the shock. No CS person running a save play. No product manager reprioritizing the roadmap. Just you, staring at a Stripe dashboard wondering if you should build the feature they asked for or ship the thing you think matters more.

The build-in-public posts celebrate the milestones. Nobody posts the Tuesday where you spend 4 hours debugging a payment webhook instead of building the thing that would actually reduce churn.

What I've learned from building solo: the product isn't the hard part. The GTM engine is. Having a repeatable way to get the next 10 customers while you're busy keeping the current 50 happy.

That's why I build systems instead of doing things manually. Content runs on a cron. Prospecting runs on a pipeline. Enrichment runs overnight. If I'm the bottleneck for every growth activity, the MRR ceiling is my available hours.

The founders who break through $10k solo are the ones who automated their own GTM before they automated their product.
posts.cta: Solo builders... what's the one operational bottleneck that caps your growth right now?

remixes.hook:
Solo founders don't have a revenue problem.

They have a fragility problem.
remixes.body:
Solo founders don't have a revenue problem.

They have a fragility problem.

Every solo business has a bus factor of one. You get sick for a week, revenue dips. Two clients churn on the same day, there's no team to absorb it. Your biggest customer asks for a feature that takes three weeks. You build it and neglect everyone else.

I've watched this pattern repeat across dozens of solo builders. They hit $3k, $5k, $8k MRR and think the hard part is over. The hard part just started.

Because now you're simultaneously the engineer, the support team, the salesperson, and the product manager. Every hour you spend on one role is an hour stolen from the others.

The fix isn't hiring. Not yet. The fix is building operational shock absorbers before you need them.

Three that made the biggest difference for me: async onboarding that doesn't require a call, a churn detection trigger that fires before the cancellation, and a weekly pipeline review that takes 15 minutes, not 2 hours.

None of these are sexy. All of them are the difference between $5k MRR that sticks and $5k MRR that evaporates the month you take a vacation.
remixes.cta: What's the one system that would keep your business running if you disappeared for two weeks?

remixes.label: the-5k-trap
remixes.hook:
There's a specific revenue range that kills more solo businesses than $0 does.

It's $4k to $7k MRR.
remixes.body:
There's a specific revenue range that kills more solo businesses than $0 does.

It's $4k to $7k MRR.

At $0, you have nothing to lose. You experiment wildly. You ship fast. You talk to every potential customer because you're hungry.

At $5k, you have just enough to cover your life. And that's when the behavior changes.

You stop experimenting because you can't afford to break what's working. You stop shipping fast because existing customers have expectations. You stop talking to new prospects because support tickets take priority.

posts.title: AI infra reselling AWS
posts.hook: Most AI infrastructure startups are middleware companies pretending to be platform companies.
posts.body:
Most AI infrastructure startups are middleware companies pretending to be platform companies.

I'm not even being contrarian. Look at the architecture. Take the API call, add a caching layer, wrap it in a nicer dashboard, charge 3x the underlying cost. That's not infrastructure. That's a skin.

The tell is the migration story. If I can swap you out in an afternoon by pointing my API calls somewhere else, you're not infrastructure. You're a convenience layer. And convenience layers get commoditized.

Real infrastructure creates lock-in through capability, not through wrapper complexity. Your data format becomes the standard. Your SDK becomes the framework. Your compute layer does something the hyperscalers genuinely can't.

I see the same pattern in GTM tooling. Products that wrap an enrichment API and charge per-seat. Products that put a UI on top of a database query. Products that are literally a Claude API call with a branded prompt.

The question I ask now before paying for any tool: what happens if this company disappears tomorrow? If the answer is "I rewrite 4 lines of code and point at the underlying API," I probably shouldn't be paying them $500/month.

Build on primitives. Rent the convenience only when the time savings justify the margin.
posts.cta: What tool in your stack would take you less than a day to replace if it disappeared?

posts.hook:
I was a plumber for ten years before I touched a line of code.

That background is the reason my systems actually work.
posts.body:
I was a plumber for ten years before I touched a line of code.

That background is the reason my systems actually work.

Tradespeople think in systems. Water comes in here, goes through this, comes out there. If the pressure is wrong, you trace the pipe back until you find the restriction. You don't guess. You diagnose.

GTM engineering is the same thing. Data comes in from signals, flows through enrichment, gets scored, routes to outreach. If conversion is low, you trace the pipeline back. Is it the data quality? The scoring model? The copy? The deliverability?

The career-pivot stories I see on LinkedIn usually frame the old career as something to escape from. "I used to be a teacher, now I build SaaS." Like the old thing was the problem.

The old thing is the advantage. A teacher knows how to explain complex ideas simply. A nurse knows triage. A plumber knows that every system is just pipes and pressure.

Coding agents changed the math on who can build software. But the people building the most useful things aren't the ones who learned to code fastest. They're the ones who brought real domain knowledge to the table and used AI to bridge the technical gap.

The background is the moat. The code is just the pipe.

The tech industry has a blind spot. It assumes the best builders come from CS programs and coding bootcamps. Some of the most effective operators I know came from trades, restaurants, logistics. They built real things with physical consequences before they ever built digital ones.

posts.title: Worst demo best inbound
posts.hook:
The YC batch company with the worst demo day pitch got the most inbound interest.

This tracks with everything I've seen in GTM.
posts.body:
The YC batch company with the worst demo day pitch got the most inbound interest.

This tracks with everything I've seen in GTM.

The polished pitch sells the vision. The rough pitch sells the problem. And buyers care about the problem.

I've written cold emails that were technically perfect. Personalized, well-structured, clear CTA. 2% reply rate. Then I wrote a scrappy 3-line email that basically said "saw you're hiring for X, we solve the exact bottleneck that role is supposed to fix, want to see it?" 11% reply rate.

The difference is legibility. The polished version signals "I'm selling to you." The rough version signals "I actually understand your situation."

Same thing happens with content. My highest-performing LinkedIn posts aren't the ones with perfect structure. They're the ones where I share a specific build detail, a real number, or an honest failure. The messier the format, the higher the engagement.

People have developed antibodies to polish. A decade of SaaS marketing trained everyone to recognize the format. The three-part framework. The clean narrative arc. The logo bar.

When something feels unpolished, it feels real. And real converts.

Stop optimizing for how good it looks. Optimize for how true it feels.
posts.cta: When was the last time something rough and honest outperformed something polished in your pipeline?
